quote: $p-q=2$ [-..-] auf $\infty$ viele Arten zu lösen, wo $p,q$ Primzahlen sind
english: To solve p - q = 2 in infinitely many ways, where p, q are primes.
topic: Notes on freeing logic and epistemology from anthropomorphic thinking, on problems whose meta-question is best settled by solving them (twin primes, digits of pi), on a philosophical theory of experimentation and meaning applied to relativity and unsolvable problems, and on the axiomatic method in physics.

triage.modern_statement: Twin prime conjecture: there are infinitely many pairs of primes (p, q) with p − q = 2. Put another way, liminf of (p_{n+1} − p_n) equals 2, where p_n is the n-th prime.
triage.answered_by: Not answered; the conjecture is still open. The best partial results are these: Chen Jingrun showed there are infinitely many primes p for which p+2 is either prime or a product of two primes. Yitang Zhang (Annals of Mathematics 179(3), 2014; announced 2013) proved that gaps between consecutive primes are bounded infinitely often, with a bound below 7×10^7. James Maynard (Nov 2013) and Terence Tao found a simpler, stronger method. The Polymath8 project, joined by Maynard, brought the bound down to H_1 ≤ 246.

evidence.claim: Hilbert's 8th problem (1900) includes the solvability of linear two-variable Diophantine equations in primes. The twin prime conjecture and the Goldbach conjecture are special cases.
The 8th of Hilbert's 23 problems includes the Riemann Hypothesis, Goldbach's conjecture and the twin prime conjecture.

Zhang proved that bounded gaps between primes occur infinitely often (Annals of Mathematics 179(3):1121-1174). Maynard simplified and strengthened the result. Chen proved that infinitely many primes p have p+2 prime or a product of two primes.
The Polymath project, with Maynard's help, reduced the bound to H_1 ≤ 246.
Tao's account of Zhang's 2013 breakthrough on bounded gaps and the Polymath work that followed.

triage.why: The note says to solve p − q = 2 in primes in infinitely many ways. That is exactly the twin prime conjecture. Hilbert named it himself in his 1900 problem 8, as a special case of linear Diophantine equations in primes. On this diary page he uses it as an example of a problem whose meta-question is best settled by solving it. It has not been solved: the bound on prime gaps stands at 246, not 2. Research is still very active, building on the Zhang–Maynard–Tao sieve methods and the Polymath8 project. Proofs that claim to settle it, like the ResearchGate paper turned up in the search, are not accepted.
